# Kakkārujātaka (Ja 326)

**ID:** Ja 326
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)

**Title (Pali):** Kakkārujātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Heavenly Pumpkin Flowers

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Kakkārujātaka* (Ja 326) is a narrative text belonging to the Jātaka collection of the Pali canon [SuttaCentral]. The framing narrative is set at Jetavana, where the Buddha refers to Devadatta, who suffered intense torment and vomited hot blood after creating a schism in the monastic order through falsehoods [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1883]. In response to the monks' discussion in the Hall of Truth, the Buddha explains that Devadatta had also been a liar in a former life and had suffered the penalties of lying [SuttaCentral].

In the story of the past, set during the reign of King Brahmadatta of Benares, the Bodhisatta was born as a deity in the Heaven of the Thirty-three (Tāvatiṃsa) [Cowell 1897]. During a grand festival in Benares, four heavenly beings descended wearing wreaths made of celestial *kakkāru* flowers, perfuming the entire city over a distance of twelve leagues [Cowell 1897]. When questioned by the assembled citizens and the king, the deities explained that such divine flowers were suitable only for beings endowed with genuine virtue and moral power, rather than the base and deceitful, prompting the eldest deity to recite the opening verse beginning *Kāyena yo nāvahare vācāya na musā bhane* ("He that from thievish act...") [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1883; Cowell 1897]. An alternate spelling, *Takkaru-jātaka*, is recorded in the index to the text [Fausböll 1897].

According to DharmaNexus, the text shares 9 matching passages (amounting to 786 characters) with the commentary in the third volume of the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus]. Neither SuttaCentral nor DharmaNexus records any cross-language parallels in Sanskrit, Chinese, or Tibetan collections [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus].
